subtype: Approach: noticing what is not working and changing the approach [Revision]
passage: Tushar, I remember a girl called Meena who joined my class when I was in Class 6. For a week she talked about how good her old school was and how many gadgets she had. Nobody sat near her. On the eighth day she looked around and noticed that whenever she began, the others went quiet. Something was not working. The next morning she said, "Rohan, what did you do on Sunday?" and listened to the whole answer. Then she asked Lata about her dog. By Friday, they had saved her a place on the bench. I'm Lokesh, and I learned from her that listening makes people come closer.

qa.q: How long did Meena talk about her old school before noticing anything?
What did Meena feel when she noticed the others going quiet?
qa.a: Meena felt puzzled and probably a bit sad, because she realised her way of talking was not working.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed things for Meena, and why?
qa.a: Meena chose to ask questions and listen instead of boasting, and that made others feel interested in and included by her.

qa.q: How might Rohan have felt when Meena asked about his Sunday?
qa.a: Rohan was probably surprised and pleased, since the new girl who used to boast now listened to his whole answer.

grounding: After a week of bragging without friends, the girl notices classmates go quiet, starts asking questions and listening, and is invited to sit with them.

subtype: Approach: noticing what is not working and changing the approach [Revision]
passage: Alka had spent her first week at the Nagpur school telling everyone how much better her old one was. By Friday, recess was cut to ten minutes because of the rain, and everyone was squeezed into the corridor. Alka noticed something: when she started talking, the girls near her went quiet and looked at each other. "They're not interested," she thought, and her ears went hot. "Maybe I'm the boring one." So she stopped. She turned to the boy next to her, Kunal, who was folding a paper boat. "How do you make it not sink?" He showed her the double fold. On Monday one of the girls waved. "Alka, sit with us. Kunal says you're good at boats."

qa.q: Why was recess cut to ten minutes?
qa.a: Recess was cut because of the rain.

qa.q: How did Alka feel when she noticed the girls go quiet?
qa.a: Alka felt embarrassed, her ears going hot, and wondered if she was the boring one.

qa.q: What else could Alka do to keep her new friendships growing?
qa.a: She could keep asking about others' interests and share her own stories only when asked, so talk goes both ways.

qa.q: How does the change in Alka look to Kunal?
qa.a: Kunal sees her asking about his paper boat and is glad to teach her, and even tells others she is good at it.

grounding: It shows a girl noticing classmates going quiet after her boasting and switching to asking questions and listening, which earns her an invitation.

subtype: Approach: noticing what is not working and changing the approach [Revision]
passage: Uma's first week at her new school in Lucknow had been one long advertisement for her old school in Delhi. Bigger rooms. Better canteen. Nicer teachers. On the second Monday she noticed that when she walked up, Parul's group went quiet. One girl looked at her shoes. Uma stood there and thought, "Every time I talk about Delhi, they stop talking." At lunch she tried something new. She asked Parul about the badge on her bag. "It's from the dance club," Parul said, and talked for five minutes about the annual show. Uma listened and asked two more questions. On Wednesday Parul saved her a seat. "You should try the dance club," she said.

qa.q: What was the badge on Parul's bag from?
qa.a: It was from the dance club.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she noticed Parul's group go quiet?
qa.a: Uma felt uncomfortable and a little ashamed, realising her talk about Delhi was pushing people away.

qa.q: Which approach worked better for Uma, and why?
qa.a: Asking Parul about the badge worked better, because people warm to someone who is interested in them.

qa.q: How does the new Uma look to Parul?
qa.a: Parul enjoys being asked about dance club and feels listened to, so she saves Uma a seat and invites her to join.

grounding: It shows a girl noticing her boasting makes classmates go quiet and switching to asking and listening, which gets her invited to sit with them.
